analysis.one_liner: Lets California enforce its own tailpipe greenhouse gas standards on cars.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 78 House members, never got a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal law, states generally cannot set their own car pollution rules; California needs a special federal waiver, which had been tied up. This bill would simply declare California's 2005 application for such a waiver approved, letting California — and any states that copy its rules — limit greenhouse gas emissions from cars and trucks. It was introduced in March 2008, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never received so much as a subcommittee vote before that Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of California and the dozen-plus states that adopt its cleaner-car standards, who would get lower tailpipe emissions of greenhouse gases and conventional pollutants over time. People would benefit through cleaner air and slower growth in transportation emissions, with any cost showing up gradually in new-vehicle prices.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Clean Air Act to deem California's December 21, 2005 application for a preemption waiver approved, removing the federal legal barrier to the state's greenhouse gas rules for vehicles.
The bill's stated purpose is to permit California and other states to effectively control greenhouse gas emissions from motor vehicles.
The measure targets climate change and motor vehicle pollution control, the subject areas listed for the bill.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would have to build and sell cleaner vehicles in California and in the states that adopt its standards rather than a single nationwide federal standard, with some share of compliance costs likely passed to new-car buyers.

drawbacks.text: Stricter state-specific standards would impose compliance costs on automakers, and those costs are typically passed at least partly to consumers as higher new-vehicle prices.

Approving California's standards by statute, rather than through the Clean Air Act's normal waiver process, would lock in a patchwork where different states have different vehicle rules — the uniformity concern the preemption rule exists to address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — cleaner air and reduced greenhouse gas emissions from the largest single source of U.S. oil demand — outweighs the cost of somewhat higher new-vehicle prices spread over years, and states that prefer the federal standard could simply not adopt California's rules. The main design criticism is procedural: hard-coding approval of one waiver application in statute sidesteps the ordinary regulatory process, though it also makes the outcome certain instead of leaving it to an agency's discretion.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its energy subcommittee, where it sat with no markup and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch introduced the Right to Clean Vehicles Act on March 6, 2008.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and then to its Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality.
The bill attracted 78 cosponsors, 75 Democrats and 3 Republicans.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote and died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers were better off, since the bill that would have forced cleaner vehicles in California and adopting states never moved. State governments seeking stricter tailpipe standards also gained nothing; the federal barrier remained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers; state clean-car rules stayed blocked

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to approve California's vehicle emissions waiver.

against.name: Rep. John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee under his chairmanship referred the bill to a subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or vote on it.

against.name: Automakers
against.what_they_did: Opposed state-level greenhouse gas standards for vehicles and pressed to keep vehicle emission rules under federal control.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 75 of 78 cosponsors were Democrats, with 3 Republicans — and the bill died in committee without any roll-call vote.

industries.note: The bill would have required car makers to meet California's stricter greenhouse gas standards in California and any adopting states, raising compliance costs. That cost is the flip side of the cleaner air the public would get, so the industry's interest ran against the bill's public benefit.
Tighter vehicle efficiency and emissions standards reduce gasoline demand over time, so the bill would have trimmed the market for transportation fuel.
